13.why: The sentence and the next one both begin "and it was given to it" (καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ). A copyist's eye could easily jump from the first to the second and leave out the words between. The sentence also repeats Daniel 7:21, which fits John's use of Daniel in this chapter.

13.a: If anyone is headed for captivity, into captivity they go.
13.t: Going into captivity, or leading others into it?
13.p: The KJV's "He that leadeth into captivity" comes from a different Greek text. This variant goes with the next one in the same verse.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: εἴ τις εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν, εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν ὑπάγει
readings.en: if anyone is for captivity, into captivity he goes
readings.plain: If anyone is headed for captivity, into captivity they go.

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity")
readings.orig: εἴ τις αἰχμαλωσίαν συνάγει, εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν ὑπάγει
readings.en: if anyone gathers into captivity, into captivity he goes
readings.plain: If anyone leads others into captivity, into captivity they go.

readings.w: The Byzantine text
readings.en: if anyone holds captives, he goes away
readings.plain: If anyone holds others captive, they will go away.

13.why: The followed reading repeats Jeremiah 15:2 (compare Jeremiah 43:11): those meant for captivity will go into captivity. The other forms turn the saying into a rule of payback, which looks like a later attempt to make the hard saying easier.

13.a: If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they must be killed.
13.t: Killed by the sword, or killing with it?
13.p: Codex Sinaiticus, the Byzantine text and the KJV read "he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword." This goes with the variant before it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: εἴ τις ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀποκτανθῆναι, αὐτὸν ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀποκτανθῆναι
readings.en: if anyone is to be killed with the sword, he is to be killed with the sword
readings.plain: If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they must be killed.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) (with the present "kills") and the Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV "he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword")
readings.orig: εἴ τις ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτενεῖ, δεῖ αὐτὸν ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτανθῆναι
readings.en: if anyone will kill with the sword, he must be killed with the sword
readings.plain: If anyone kills with the sword, by the sword they must be killed.

13.why: NA28 and SBLGNT follow Alexandrinus: its Greek is rough, which is why copyists would smooth it, and it keeps the pattern of Jeremiah 15:2 and the first half of the verse. Read this way, the verse tells the saints to accept suffering. The other reading, close to Jesus' words in Matthew 26:52, warns them not to take up the sword. Both lead to the same call: "This is where the saints show their endurance."
13.b: Some editions (Westcott-Hort, Tregelles and the Tyndale House Greek New Testament) print "must" (δεῖ) in the second half, with the Byzantine text. The 13:9–10 card on this chapter page gives the setting.

13.p: The KJV makes the name a second, separate option.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: τὸ χάραγμα, τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θηρίου
readings.en: the mark, the name of the beast

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "the mark, or the name of the beast")
readings.orig: τὸ χάραγμα, ἢ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θηρίου
readings.en: the mark, or the name of the beast
readings.plain: the mark, or the beast's name

13.why: In this text the mark is the beast's name or its number, not a third thing beside them.

13.p: The oldest surviving copy of this verse reads 616. Nearly all others read 666.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile), both in words; the Byzantine text; Irenaeus; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT; the Textus Receptus (as a numeral, χξϛʹ)

P115 (P.Oxy. 4499, a fragment from about AD 300 and the oldest surviving copy of the verse) and Codex Ephraemi (400s), both as reported by Daniel B. Wallace; copies known to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.1)
Minuscule 2344, a later manuscript (listed in published summaries of the variants)

13.why: 666 has by far the widest support, and Irenaeus, about AD 180, said it stood in all the good and ancient copies, while he knew of copies with 616 and thought them a mistake. Still, 616 is very old, and it fits a known explanation: "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters adds up to 666 when spelled נרון קסר and to 616 when spelled the Latin way, נרו קסר. Many scholars think a copyist who knew the Nero reading adjusted the number to the Latin spelling.
13.b: On what "a human number" means, see the note on those words and the 13:16–18 card.

14.a: his name and the name of his Father
14.p: The KJV has only "his Father's name."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: his name and the name of his Father
readings.plain: his name and the name of his Father

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "having his Father's name written in their foreheads")

14.why: The shorter reading is in none of the editions compared here except the Textus Receptus; the eye could skip from the first "name" to the second. The KJV also says "a Lamb," where the Greek has "the Lamb."

14.p: The critical editions and the KJV have "as it were" (ὡς); Codex Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text do not.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT; Textus Receptus (KJV "they sung as it were a new song")
readings.en: they sing as it were a new song

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text

14.why: The Plain follows its base text, SBLGNT. "As it were" fits John's way of describing what he hears ("like the roar of many waters," 14:2), and a copyist may have dropped it to match 5:9. The evidence is divided.

14.p: The KJV adds "before the throne of God," which none of the other editions has.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT (the Byzantine text adds "for")
Textus Receptus (KJV "for they are without fault before the throne of God")
readings.orig: ἄμωμοι γάρ εἰσιν ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.en: for they are without fault before the throne of God
readings.plain: For they are without blemish before the throne of God.

14.why: The added words are an expansion, perhaps from Jude 24, where God presents believers "without blemish" before his glory.

14.p: The Byzantine text has the cry once; the KJV has it twice and adds "that great city."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT; Textus Receptus
The Byzantine text; a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus, who supplied the missing cry (its first copyist skipped it; Tischendorf's edition)

14.why: The double cry follows Isaiah 21:9, which this verse quotes, and 18:2 repeats it.
14.b: The Textus Receptus also reads "Babylon is fallen, is fallen, that great city" (KJV), adding "city" (ἡ πόλις); none of the other editions has it.

15.p: The KJV adds "and over his mark."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Textus Receptus (KJV "and over his image, and over his mark")
readings.orig: ἐκ τῆς εἰκόνος αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ χαράγματος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: over its image and over its mark
readings.plain: over its image, over its mark

15.why: "His mark" is a natural addition from 13:16–17 and 14:9; Codex Sinaiticus and the critical and Byzantine editions lack it.

15.t: King of the nations, of the ages, or of the saints?
15.p: Here the Plain departs from its base text, SBLGNT, which reads "King of the ages." The KJV says "King of saints."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, THGNT, Tregelles
Codex Sinaiticus as first written (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
The Textus Receptus (KJV "thou King of saints")

15.why: The song draws on Jeremiah 10:7, "King of the nations," and goes straight on to "All the nations will come and worship" (15:4), so "nations" fits the context; it is in Alexandrinus and the Byzantine text, and NA28 prints it. "King of the ages" is what Sinaiticus first read and is a real possibility; it may have come in from 1 Timothy 1:17. "Saints" is in none of the editions compared here except the Textus Receptus.

15.t: Dressed in linen, or in stone?
15.p: Codex Alexandrinus says the angels were dressed in pure, bright stone.

readings.w: The Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus (Codex Sinaiticus, in Tischendorf's edition, has a related form: "pure, bright linen garments")
Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), which reads ΛΙΘΟΝ; some Latin Vulgate texts (lapide; the Clementine Vulgate has lino, "linen"); Westcott-Hort, Tregelles

15.why: In Greek capitals the two words differ by one letter (ΛΙΝΟΝ, ΛΙΘΟΝ), and most editors judge "stone" a copying slip. But it is the harder reading and the reading of Alexandrinus: some compare the king of Tyre dressed in precious stones (Ezekiel 28:13). Westcott-Hort and Tregelles print it; the other editions set it aside.

16.a: the one who is and who was
16.p: No known Greek manuscript has "and shalt be." It came from the editor Theodore Beza.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, the Byzantine text
readings.orig: ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν, ὁ ὅσιος
readings.en: who is and who was, the Holy One
readings.plain: the one who is and who was

readings.w: Theodore Beza, who proposed it in his Latin translation and notes (checked in his 1588 edition), saying he had restored it from an old manuscript; the Textus Receptus behind the KJV follows him (KJV "O Lord, which art, and wast, and shalt be")
readings.orig: ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος
readings.en: who is and who was and who will be
readings.plain: the one who is and who was and who will be

16.why: Beza argued in his notes that "the Holy One" broke the pattern of 1:4 and 1:8 and that John must have written "who will be"; he claimed an old manuscript for it, but none is known today, and the Textus Receptus and the KJV followed him. The Greek manuscripts and editions read "who is and who was, the Holy One." The missing third part is deliberate on John's part; see the note on "and who was."
16.b: In Beza's 1588 edition the Greek column itself still prints καὶ ὁ ὅσιος, "and the Holy One," after "O Lord" (Κύριε); "who will be" appears in his Latin translation and his note.

16.t: The altar speaks, or someone at it?
16.p: The KJV has "another out of the altar," a voice from the altar rather than the altar itself.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Textus Receptus (KJV "I heard another out of the altar say")
readings.orig: ἤκουσα ἄλλου ἐκ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου λέγοντος
readings.en: I heard another from the altar saying
readings.plain: another voice from the altar say

16.why: The Textus Receptus smooths a bold image. In the Greek the altar itself, where the martyrs' souls cried out (6:9–10), answers that God's judgments are just.

16.a: the kings of the whole world
16.t: "Of the earth and of the whole world"

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.en: the kings of the whole world
readings.plain: the kings of the whole world

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "the kings of the earth and of the whole world")
readings.orig: τοὺς βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς καὶ τῆς οἰκουμένης ὅλης
readings.en: the kings of the earth and of the whole world
readings.plain: the kings of the earth and of the whole world

16.why: "The kings of the earth" is a familiar phrase in Revelation (17:2; 18:3), so "of the earth" was easily added.

16.p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say "out of the temple of heaven."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition, "out of the temple of God"); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
The Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV "out of the temple of heaven")
readings.plain: out of the temple of heaven

16.why: The meaning is the same, since the temple is in heaven (15:5); "of heaven" spells it out.

16.p: NA28 reads the singular, "since a human being came to be on the earth," perhaps a hint at Adam.

readings.w: SBLGNT, the Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "since men were upon the earth")
NA28 (and Tregelles)
readings.en: since a human being came to be
readings.plain: since a human being came to be

16.why: The Plain follows its base text, SBLGNT. The difference is small: either way, no earthquake like it has happened in all human history (compare Daniel 12:1).

6.p: Codex Alexandrinus and the critical editions have one word, "Come!" Codex Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text add "and see." The same choice returns at 6:3, 5 and 7.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "Come and see")

6.why: The short reading is in Codex Alexandrinus and every critical edition, and the addition is easy to explain: a copyist took the command as spoken to John, who looks next, and added "and see." No one would have reason to drop the words if they were original.
6.b: The choice decides who is spoken to. Without the addition, each living creature calls a rider out onto the stage of history. With it, John is invited to come and look. Codex Vaticanus, one of the oldest Greek Bibles, does not contain Revelation.

6.p: Goes with the variant at 6:1: Codex Alexandrinus, the editions and here the Byzantine text have "Come!" alone; Codex Sinaiticus adds "and see," and the KJV has "Come and see."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition)
Textus Receptus (KJV "Come and see")

6.why: As at 6:1: the short reading has the best support, and the addition makes the command an invitation to John.

6.p: Goes with the variant at 6:1: the critical editions have "Come!" alone; Codex Sinaiticus, the Byzantine text and the KJV add "and see."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "Come and see")

6.why: As at 6:1: the short reading has the best support, and the addition makes the command an invitation to John.

6.p: Goes with the variant at 6:1: the critical editions have "Come!" alone; Codex Sinaiticus, the Byzantine text and the KJV add "and see."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "Come and see")

6.why: As at 6:1: the short reading has the best support, and the addition makes the command an invitation to John.

6.t: Given to them, or to him?
6.p: The Byzantine text gives the power to Death alone; the other texts give it to Death and Hades together.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Textus Receptus (KJV "power was given unto them")
Byzantine text

6.why: The plural is in Codex Sinaiticus and every edition except the Byzantine. The singular looks like a correction to fit the single rider, since Hades is only following.

6.p: The Byzantine text says it was "the testimony of the Lamb" that the martyrs held.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) (ἣν ἔσχον); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Textus Receptus (KJV "the testimony which they held")
Byzantine text
readings.orig: τὴν μαρτυρίαν τοῦ ἀρνίου ἣν εἶχον
readings.en: the testimony of the Lamb which they held
readings.plain: the testimony of the Lamb that they held

6.why: The shorter text is in every edition but the Byzantine. The addition spells out whose testimony is meant, as 12:17 and 19:10 speak of the testimony of Jesus.

6.t: Until they are completed, or until they complete their course?
6.p: Two modern editions differ: the number of martyrs is filled up, or the martyrs finish their course.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort
Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text

6.why: The passive is the harder Greek ("until their fellow slaves are completed"), and a copyist could have smoothed it into the active. The editors of NA28 and SBLGNT judge it original; the Tyndale House editors prefer the active. The sense is close either way.
6.b: The Plain supplies "in number" to make the passive clear; the Greek says only "until they are completed." The idea that God waits until a set number of the righteous or the martyrs is reached also appears in 1 Enoch 47:4 and 4 Ezra 4:35–37. The KJV's "should be fulfilled" gives the same sense as the Plain.

6.p: Modern editions read "their anger," God's and the Lamb's together. The KJV has "his wrath."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "his wrath")

6.why: "Their" is the harder reading: it joins the Lamb to the one on the throne as sharers in one anger (6:16), something a copyist was more likely to smooth into "his" than to create. The critical editions print it.
6.b: Even with "his," the Lamb's anger is named in 6:16. The plural fits the book's habit of setting God and the Lamb side by side (5:13; 7:10; 22:1).

7.a: out of the tribe of Reuben, 12,000; out of the tribe of Gad, 12,000;
7.p: The KJV repeats "were sealed" after each tribe. The Greek of the modern editions has it only after Judah and Benjamin.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
readings.en: of the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand
readings.plain: out of the tribe of Reuben, 12,000; out of the tribe of Gad, 12,000;

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "were sealed twelve thousand" each time)
readings.orig: ἐκ φυλῆς Ῥουβὴν δώδεκα χιλιάδες ἐσφραγισμένοι
readings.en: of the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand sealed
readings.plain: out of the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 were sealed; out of the tribe of Gad, 12,000 were sealed;

7.why: The modern editions and the Byzantine text say "sealed" only at the start (Judah) and the end (Benjamin), framing the list. The Textus Receptus fills it in after every tribe, the kind of regularizing copyists often did. The meaning does not change.

8.a: a third of the earth burned up, and
8.t: Missing from the KJV: "a third of the earth burned up"
8.p: The KJV lacks the first of the three "burned up" clauses.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
readings.orig: καὶ τὸ τρίτον τῆς γῆς κατεκάη
readings.en: and a third of the earth was burned up
readings.plain: a third of the earth burned up, and

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV)

8.why: The clause is in every modern edition and in the Byzantine text. Its absence from the Textus Receptus is most likely an accident: the eye of a copyist could easily skip from one "burned up" (katekaē) to the next, since the word ends all three clauses.

8.p: The KJV says "an angel," but the two oldest manuscripts and the Byzantine text say "an eagle."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
The Textus Receptus (KJV "an angel")

8.why: "Eagle" is in the two oldest manuscripts and every edition except the Textus Receptus. "Angel" is an easy change: the two Greek words look alike (aetou, angelou), and angels fly in midheaven elsewhere in the book (14:6), so a copyist expecting an angel could write one.
8.b: The Greek aetos also means vulture, and vultures gather over the dead (Matthew 24:28). Hosea 8:1 pictures an eagle over God's house with a trumpet to the lips, a fitting herald for the last three trumpets. The eagle is also one of the four living creatures (4:7).

9.p: The editions disagree on whether the altar's horns are called "four." The Plain follows its base text, the SBLGNT.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
NA28, the Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the four horns")

9.why: The manuscripts are divided, and so are the editors. "Four" may have been added to answer the four angels of 9:14, or dropped because an altar's horns were known to be four (Exodus 27:2; Exodus 30:2–3). The Plain keeps to the SBLGNT; the meaning is the same either way.
9.b: Codex Sinaiticus as first written has neither form: it reads only "a voice of the gold altar," and a corrector added "one, from the horns" (Tischendorf's edition).

9.p: The Byzantine text has "myriads of myriads," a countless host, not an exact 200 million.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "two hundred thousand thousand")

9.why: The rare word dismyriades, "double myriads," is the harder reading; copyists could easily turn it into the familiar "myriads of myriads" of 5:11 and Daniel 7:10.
9.b: The difference matters to readers who build on the exact figure (see the note on 9:16). The KJV's number is the same as the Plain's.

9.p: Modern editions read pharmaka, "potions, spells"; the Byzantine text and the KJV have pharmakeia, "sorceries."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort
Tregelles, the Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "sorceries")

9.why: Pharmakeia is the more common word and the one John uses at 18:23, so a copyist could easily have changed the rarer pharmaka to it. The meaning is nearly the same: both are about magic.

10.p: The Byzantine text says only "a mighty angel." The word "another" matters to the question of who this angel is.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Textus Receptus (KJV "another mighty angel")
Byzantine text

10.why: "Another" is in every edition except the Byzantine, and it links this angel to the mighty angel of 5:2.
10.b: Readers who argue that the angel is not Christ often point to "another": he is one more angel like the one in 5:2 (see the note on 10:1).

10.p: Here Codex Alexandrinus and the modern editions say simply "the scroll"; Codex Sinaiticus, the Byzantine text and the KJV make it "the little scroll," as in 10:2, 9 and 10.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) (βιβλαρίδιον); Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV "the little book which is open")
readings.orig: τὸ βιβλιδάριον (Byzantine) / τὸ βιβλαρίδιον (TR) τὸ ἠνεῳγμένον

10.why: The plain word biblion is the harder reading in a chapter that otherwise says "little scroll"; copyists made it match.
10.b: Bauckham uses this verse to argue that the "little scroll" is the same scroll the Lamb took in chapter 5, now opened and given to John.

11.p: The Greek has only "saying," with no speaker. The KJV adds "and the angel stood."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
A later corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); Textus Receptus (KJV "and the angel stood, saying")
readings.plain: and the angel stood there and said

11.why: The words are not in Codex Sinaiticus as first written, in the critical editions or in the Byzantine text. They look like a clarification that gives the loose participle "saying" a subject.

11.t: The Lord or the God of the earth?
11.p: The KJV has "the God of the earth." Every other text has "Lord," as in Zechariah 4:14.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "the God of the earth")

11.why: "Lord" has the manuscript support and matches Zechariah 4:14, which John is echoing, where the olive trees stand by the Lord of all the earth.

11.p: In the Byzantine text John hears the voice; in the other texts the two witnesses hear it.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as first written, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Ephraemi and Codex P (as Tischendorf's 1865 edition notes); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Textus Receptus (KJV "they heard")
Byzantine text

11.why: The two forms differ by one letter. "I heard" is John's habit all through the book, which could easily draw a copyist to it; "they heard" fits the scene, where the call is spoken "to them."

11.p: The KJV has "the kingdoms of this world." The Greek manuscripts have one kingdom, the world's, which changes hands.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text

11.why: Both of the oldest manuscripts have the shorter title, and so does the Byzantine text. The longer one copies the familiar threefold title of 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8, exactly the kind of change copyists made.
11.b: The shorter title is one of the book's most meaningful small details. At the seventh trumpet God is no longer "the one who is coming": he has come, and has taken up his reign. Bauckham, Beale and Koester all read the omission as deliberate. The same shortened title returns at 16:5.

1.p: The oldest manuscripts say Jesus "loves" us, in the present. The KJV says "loved."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's 1865 edition), Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT

1.why: The present is in both of the oldest manuscripts of the book and in every edition except the Textus Receptus. It is also the harder reading next to the past tense "set us free": a scribe was more likely to make both verbs past than to make one present.
1.b: The present tense makes a point: Christ's love goes on now, while his freeing act was done once.

1.p: The oldest manuscripts say he "freed" us from our sins. Later ones, and the KJV, say he "washed" us.

1.why: "Freed" is the reading of the two oldest manuscripts of the book and of every critical edition. In Greek the two words differ by one letter (lysanti, lousanti), and "washed" may have come in from the robes washed in the Lamb's blood in 7:14.
1.b: "Freed" also fits the next verse, where a people freed from Egypt is made a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6). Both readings are true to the book; the question is only which John wrote here.

The Textus Receptus (KJV "we shall reign")

5.why: This is one of the few places where the Plain leaves the SBL text. The future is in Codex Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text, and the book's promises of reigning point forward (20:4–6; 22:5). The present is Alexandrinus's reading, often strong in Revelation, which is why SBL and Westcott and Hort print it; the NA28 and Tyndale House editors judge the future more likely original.
5.b: The choice touches the millennium debate. Premillennialists favor the future, pointing to the thousand-year reign of 20:4–6. Amillennialists note that the present fits 1:6, where believers are already a kingdom, and read the reign as happening now. Both readings are possible Greek, and the two oldest manuscripts split. The KJV's "we" goes with its "us" in 5:9–10.

18.why: The site's base text, the SBLGNT, prints the longer form, and NA28 prints it too. The repeated words "a prison of every unclean..." make it easy for a copyist's eye to jump from one to the next and drop a line; on the other hand, a scribe could have added the third line to round out the picture of Isaiah 13:21–22 and 34:11–14. Tyndale House prints the shorter form.
18.b: The cry "Fallen, fallen" is doubled in NA28, SBLGNT and the Textus Receptus, as in Isaiah 21:9; Codex Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text have "Fallen" once. Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile) has yet another form: a prison for every unclean and hated spirit and a prison for every unclean and hated beast, with no bird line.

18.p: The Plain follows NA28 ("have drunk") against its own base text, the SBLGNT ("have fallen"). The two Greek words differ by one letter.

18.why: The better-attested reading is "have fallen (by the wine)," and the SBLGNT prints it. The Plain follows NA28's "have drunk" because it fits the picture the book has already drawn: Babylon "made all the nations drink" her wine (14:8), and those who live on the earth "were made drunk" with it (17:2). The two words differ by one letter (pepōkan, pepṭōkan), and "fallen" may have come in from "Fallen, fallen" one verse earlier. This is a close call, and readers should know the main manuscripts say "fallen."

19.why: "Our" has the support of Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text, and it matches "our God" in 19:1 and 19:5; NA28 and Tyndale House print it. The SBLGNT leaves it out. The meaning hardly changes.

19.a: wears a robe dipped in blood
19.p: Codex Sinaiticus and Westcott-Hort say the robe was "sprinkled" with blood.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "dipped in blood")
readings.plain: wears a robe dipped in blood

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand περιρεραμμένον, a corrector περιρεραντισμένον; Tischendorf's edition); Westcott-Hort (ῥεραντισμένον)
readings.en: a garment sprinkled (all over) with blood
readings.plain: wears a robe sprinkled with blood

19.why: "Dipped" is the harder word and best explains the others: copyists seem to have softened it, or brought it closer to the spattered garments of Isaiah 63:3 and the sprinkling of blood in the Law. Even within Sinaiticus a corrector changed the spelling, a sign of later tinkering.
19.b: The choice touches the debate in the note on this verse: a robe "dipped" in blood before the battle is soaked through, which many read as the rider's own blood.

20.a: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were finished.
20.p: Codex Sinaiticus leaves out the first sentence of 20:5.

readings.w: The Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔζησαν ἄχρι τελεσθῇ τὰ χίλια ἔτη.
readings.en: the rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed
readings.plain: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were finished.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition)

20.why: The sentence is in every edition. Its loss is easy to explain: 20:4 and the sentence both end with "a thousand years" (chilia etē), so a copyist's eye could jump from the first ending to the second.
20.b: The sentence matters for the millennium debate. Without it there is no explicit second group raised after the thousand years, and premillennial readers lean on it for two resurrections a thousand years apart. Amillennial readers point out that the KJV and most Bibles print it, and that "came to life" can be read in more than one way (see the notes on 20:4 and 20:5).

20.t: "From heaven" or "from God out of heaven"?
20.p: Many manuscripts and the KJV add "from God."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT
The Byzantine text; Tregelles
readings.orig: ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.plain: came down from heaven, from God

readings.w: A corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (its first copyist skipped the whole passage; checked in Tischendorf's edition); Textus Receptus (KJV "came down from God out of heaven")
readings.orig: ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
readings.plain: came down from God out of heaven

20.why: "From God" turns up in different places in different manuscripts, which is the usual sign of an addition. The short reading also matches the fire that came down from heaven in 2 Kings 1:10–12, which the verse echoes.

20.a: This is the second death, the lake of fire.
20.t: "The lake of fire" at the end?
20.p: The KJV ends the verse at "This is the second death."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in Tischendorf's edition), the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: οὗτος ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερός ἐστιν, ἡ λίμνη τοῦ πυρός.
readings.en: this is the second death, the lake of fire
readings.plain: This is the second death, the lake of fire.

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "This is the second death")

20.why: The closing words are in Codex Sinaiticus and every edition except the Textus Receptus; the Textus Receptus seems to have lost them because the sentence before also ends with "the lake of fire."

21.p: The two oldest manuscripts have the plural, "peoples," which breaks the old formula "my people."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT; also the Textus Receptus
The Byzantine text; the KJV's "his people" (which may simply render the plural)

21.why: The plural is the harder reading: the familiar promise is "you will be my people," singular (Leviticus 26:12; Ezekiel 37:27), and copyists would tend to bring the verse back to it. The plural makes the point that the people of God now come from many nations (5:9; 7:9).

21.a: God himself will be with them and be their God
21.p: The Plain follows NA28 and Tyndale House in printing "and be their God." The SBLGNT, Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text lack it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "and be their God")
readings.orig: καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς μετ’ αὐτῶν ἔσται αὐτῶν θεός
readings.en: and God himself will be with them, their God
readings.plain: God himself will be with them and be their God

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in Tischendorf's edition), the Byzantine text; SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς μετ’ αὐτῶν ἔσται
readings.en: and God himself will be with them
readings.plain: God himself will be with them

21.why: A close call. The words could have been added to complete the covenant formula ("I will be your God"), or dropped because they seemed to repeat "with them" (meta autōn ... autōn). NA28 and Tyndale House print them; the site's base text, the SBLGNT, does not. The Plain keeps them, so this entry marks a place where it leaves the SBLGNT.

21.a: It has all happened. I am the Alpha and the Omega
21.t: "It has happened," "I have become," or "It is done"?
21.p: Three forms of one Greek verb, and three meanings.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.orig: Γέγοναν. ἐγώ τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ
readings.en: They have happened. I am the Alpha and the Omega
readings.plain: It has all happened. I am the Alpha and the Omega

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) (γέγονα ἐγὼ τὸ ἄλφα), the Byzantine text
readings.orig: Γέγονα τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ
readings.en: I have become the Alpha and the Omega
readings.plain: I have become the Alpha and the Omega

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "It is done. I am Alpha and Omega")
readings.orig: Γέγονε. ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω
readings.en: It is done. I am the Alpha and the Omega
readings.plain: It is done. I am the Alpha and the Omega

21.why: "They have happened" (plural) is unusual and the hardest to explain as a copyist's change; the singular forms look like smoothings. It refers back to "these words" of 21:5: everything God promised has come to pass. Compare the single word from the throne in 16:17.

21.p: The KJV's "that great city, the holy Jerusalem" follows the later text.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); NA28, SBLGNT
The Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "that great city, the holy Jerusalem")
readings.orig: τὴν πόλιν τὴν μεγάλην τὴν ἁγίαν Ἰερουσαλήμ
readings.en: the great city, the holy Jerusalem
readings.plain: the great city, the holy Jerusalem

21.why: In Revelation "the great city" is Babylon (17:18; 18:10). Codex Sinaiticus and the critical editions call the new Jerusalem "the holy city" only (as in 21:2); "great" was probably added by copyists who knew the phrase.

21.t: "The nations of those who are saved"?
21.p: The KJV narrows "the nations" to "the nations of them which are saved."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT
The Textus Receptus (KJV "the nations of them which are saved shall walk")
readings.en: the nations of those who are saved will walk
readings.plain: The nations of those who are saved will walk

21.why: The phrase is in none of the editions compared here except the Textus Receptus. It looks like an explanation that entered the text, perhaps from a commentary, to make sure "the nations" were understood as the saved.
21.b: It matters: the open "the nations" is what leads many readers to see hope for the nations here (see the note on the kings of the earth).

22.a: showed me a river of the water of life
22.p: The KJV's "a pure river" follows the later text.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); NA28, SBLGNT
readings.en: a river of water of life
readings.plain: showed me a river of the water of life

readings.w: The Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "a pure river of water of life")
readings.en: a pure river of water of life
readings.plain: showed me a pure river of the water of life

22.why: "Pure" is not in Codex Sinaiticus or the critical editions; it fits the city's "pure gold" (21:18, 21) and was easily added.

22.a: Let the righteous go on doing righteousness
22.p: The KJV's "let him be righteous still" comes from the Textus Receptus.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in Tischendorf's edition), the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT
readings.en: let the righteous still do righteousness
readings.plain: Let the righteous go on doing righteousness

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "let him be righteous still")
readings.en: let the righteous still be made righteous
readings.plain: Let the righteous go on being made righteous

22.why: The Textus Receptus form matches the passive verbs of the other three lines, which is just the kind of change copyists made; the manuscripts have "do righteousness."

22.a: Blessed are those who wash their robes
22.p: The KJV's "Blessed are they that do his commandments" follows the Byzantine text.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), with the Latin Vulgate (qui lavant stolas suas); NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: μακάριοι οἱ πλύνοντες τὰς στολὰς αὐτῶν
readings.en: blessed are those who wash their robes
readings.plain: Blessed are those who wash their robes

readings.w: The Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: μακάριοι οἱ ποιοῦντες τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: blessed are those who do his commandments
readings.plain: Blessed are those who do his commandments

22.why: The two oldest Greek manuscripts have "wash their robes," which ties back to 7:14 ("they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb"). Written in capitals with no spaces, as scribes wrote, the two readings look alike: ΠΛΥΝΟΝΤΕΣΤΑΣΣΤΟΛΑΣ and ΠΟΙΟΥΝΤΕΣΤΑΣΕΝΤΟΛΑΣ. A tired copyist could slip, and keeping the commandments of God is a theme John returns to (12:17; 14:12).
22.b: The difference shapes the verse. "Wash their robes" makes entry a gift received; "do his commandments" makes it faithful obedience. Revelation holds both together elsewhere (12:17; 14:12; 22:7).

22.p: The KJV's "book of life" goes back to Erasmus, who translated the last verses of the book into Greek from the Latin.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT
Erasmus's Greek New Testament (1516), which supplied 22:16–21 by translating from the Latin; Textus Receptus (KJV "out of the book of life")

22.why: None of the Greek editions compared here reads "book" except the Textus Receptus. Latin texts differ here between ligno ("tree") and libro ("book"); Erasmus's Greek follows "book," and the Textus Receptus kept it.
22.b: When Erasmus prepared the first Greek New Testament to be published (1516), his only manuscript of Revelation was a twelfth-century copy with the commentary of Andrew of Caesarea (now called minuscule 2814). It had lost its last leaf, with 22:16–21. Erasmus filled the gap by translating the Latin back into Greek, and some of his words stayed in the Textus Receptus behind the KJV. Two reach the KJV here: "book of life" in this verse, and "with you all" in 22:21. Other wording in these verses also differs from every Greek manuscript (for example, the Textus Receptus has ἐλθέ for ἔρχου, "come," in 22:17).

22.p: The last words have four forms in the manuscripts, and Codex Alexandrinus lacks "Amen."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), without "Amen"; NA28, SBLGNT
Codex Sinaiticus (checked in Tischendorf's edition); Tyndale House GNT (Westcott-Hort print "with the saints" without "Amen")
The Byzantine text, which also reads "the Lord Jesus Christ"
Textus Receptus (KJV "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen"), from Erasmus's back-translation

22.why: The SBLGNT and NA28 follow Codex Alexandrinus, which has the short "with all" and no "Amen." "Amen" is the kind of word copyists added at the end of a book read in church, and "the saints" may come from the usual close of letters. Tyndale House follows Sinaiticus. The KJV's "with you all" has almost no Greek support: it comes from Erasmus's Latin-based Greek (see 22:19).
